new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable, stated explicitly only for disyllabic words; nothing is said about longer words. The same author (1971: 85) adds for the Kayagar family that the syllabic nasal of word-final /pm/, /tn/ clusters can itself carry the stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; statement restricted to bisyllabic words. Voorhoeve 1971: 85 (family-level): nasal in final /pm/, /tn/ clusters 'can carry stress'. (Second-hand data point: Clouse 1987 forms as reproduced on NewGuineaWorld show mostly final stress marks with at least one initial-stressed item, 'pErum 'rattan'.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from elicited wordlist items (1970 fieldtrip lists of Sinepit = Cook River dialect and Jakamit = Kronkel River dialect); the ü/ö vowels in the 1975 inventory belong to the Cook River dialect (1971: 85 says they are absent from the Kronkel River dialect). No phrase-level information.
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve's 'Kaugat' is the same language as Glottolog atoh1238 Atohwaim [aqm] (Glottolog alt name Kaugat; Usher: 'Atohaim (Atohwaim, Atoheim), known also as Kaugat'). Voorhoeve's data come from Sinepit (Cook River dialect) and Jakamit (Kronkel River dialect), 5 villages, c. 700 speakers (1970); the 1975 inventory with ü, ö reflects the Cook River dialect. Not to be confused with Kayagar/Kaygir [kyt] or Tamagario [tcg], the sister Gondu River languages, for which Voorhoeve gives the identical final-stress sentence.

sources.note: Sec. 3.2 'The Kajagar Family' pp. 79-88, phoneme inventories for Kaugat/Kaigir/Tamagario pp. 82-85; Distribution p. 85: word-final clusters /pm/, /tn/ only, 'the nasal in these clusters can carry stress'. No stress-placement rule; Appendix II Kaugat wordlists (pp. 110-114, Sinepit and Jakamit) carry no stress marks.

sources.note: Sister-group comparative page: 'Stress generally falls on the final syllable of nominals, as Cook and Gondu River unstressed final vowels have been dropped. In Yogo there has been a trend towards initial stress.' Cites Voorhoeve 1971: 85 on stressable syllabic nasals. Not a first-hand Atohwaim statement.
Lexical data only (135 items from Voorhoeve 1971, 1975); nothing on stress.
